name: Sauna / sweat suits

image.caption: Home Bath Sauna Suit - Don Quijote, Roppongi

lead: Sauna suits and saunas make people sweat heavily, and they are used for quick scale-weight drops, especially before weigh-ins in combat sports. Users also sweat to look drier and leaner for a day, and some believe the sweating burns fat.

The garment or room limits heat loss, raising body temperature and sweat output. The weight lost is mostly water and returns with rehydration. A 2022 survey of elite judo athletes described rapid loss followed by rapid regain as a regular pre-competition routine; lab studies have measured sauna suit effects on body temperature, sweat and energy expenditure.

paras: Users wear a non-breathable suit while exercising or rest in a heated room, then rehydrate afterward. The scale change shows within hours.
Heat strain and dehydration are the general concerns of heat exposure; rapid fluid loss is associated with both. The sources reviewed give limited detail on adverse outcomes.

angle.text: Heavy sweating in a sauna or sweat suit drops water weight, giving a drier, leaner look for a day. The weight change shows on the scale and returns with rehydration, and direct fat-loss research is limited.

lead: Sauna suits are non-breathable garments, and saunas are heated rooms, used while exercising or resting to provoke heavy sweating. Practitioners use them for temporary weight loss and in some circles believe the sweating burns fat or flushes it out; the weight lost is mostly water, which returns with rehydration.

In sport, deliberate sweating is a recognized method of rapid weight loss before weigh-ins, and a 2022 survey of elite judo athletes described such rapid loss followed by rapid regain as a regular pre-competition routine in combat sports and weightlifting.[1] Controlled laboratory work on sauna suits has measured their effects on body temperature, sweat and energy expenditure during exercise.[2][3]

paras: A sauna suit is an upper-body or full-body garment designed to restrict heat loss during exercise. Studies describe such restrictive heat-loss attire as a way to raise heat strain at a given workload.[2]

sections.h: Use in combat sports and weight cutting
paras: Rapid weight loss before competition is common in weight-class sports. A survey of 138 elite judokas, published in 2022 in the Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition, examined methods and nutrition around rapid weight loss and regain in relation to competition performance.[1] The abstract available for this entry does not list the specific methods used.

A 2018 crossover experiment in ten moderately trained people had participants cycle for 30 minutes in temperate and hot conditions with and without an upper-body sauna suit, measuring physiological and perceptual responses.[2] A 2022 study in the Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research examined energy expenditure and excess post-exercise oxygen consumption during high-intensity interval exercise while wearing a sauna suit.[3] The results sections of these abstracts were not available for this entry, so their findings are not summarised here.
Separately, a 2018 trial in nine women reported that sauna exposure before heat-acclimation sessions accelerated heat adaptation; that study concerned heat tolerance, not fat loss.[4]
